Text: A codon is {{c1::three mRNA nucleotides that specify one amino acid}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "This conversion is governed by the genetic code, the specification of amino acids by nucleotide triplets called codons in the gene transcript."

Cue: the UUU triplet in an mRNA specifies phenylalanine (Phe); three of the 64 codons signal 'stop' instead of an amino acid.

Formal: "A set of three adjacent nucleotides in an mRNA molecule that specifies the incorporation of an amino acid into a polypeptide chain or that signals the end of polypeptide synthesis."

Text: A primary transcript is {{c1::the RNA exactly as transcribed, before any processing}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "In prokaryotes, the product of transcription, the primary transcript, usually is equivalent to the mRNA molecule."

Distinguish: in eukaryotes the primary transcript is the pre-mRNA; the mature mRNA is what is left after capping, tailing and splicing, so the two are the same molecule only in prokaryotes.

Formal: "The RNA molecule produced by transcription prior to any posttranscriptional modifications; also called a pre-mRNA in eukaryotes."

Text: A promoter is {{c1::where RNA polymerase binds DNA to start transcription}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "RNA polymerases bind to specific nucleotide sequences called promoters, and with the help of proteins called transcription factors, initiate the synthesis of RNA molecules at transcription start sites near the promoters."

Distinguish: the promoter sits in the DNA just upstream of the transcription start site (+1); it is a binding site, not part of the message that gets transcribed.

Pitfall: the same word has an unrelated second sense (a chemical that pushes benign cells toward cancer); in transcription it always means the polymerase-binding sequence.

Text: Archaea are {{c1::the prokaryotes that are not bacteria}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The RNA polymerases of archaea have quite different structures; they will not be discussed here."

Distinguish: bacteria and archaea are the two kinds of prokaryote (no nucleus); E. coli is a bacterium, so the single five-subunit RNA polymerase described for it is the bacterial enzyme, not the archaeal one.

Cue: introns turn up in some archaeal genes, which is one reason the book keeps archaea apart from bacteria.

Text: The nucleolus is {{c1::the nuclear region that makes rRNA and ribosomes}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "RNA polymerase I is located in the nucleolus, a distinct region of the nucleus where rRNAs are synthesized and combined with ribosomal proteins."

Distinguish: the nucleolus is a region, not a membrane-bound organelle; the rest of the nucleus (where RNA polymerases II and III work) is simply called the nucleus.

Formal: "An RNA-rich, spherical sack in the nucleus of metabolic cells; associated with the nucleolar organizer; storage place for ribosomes and ribosome precursors."

Text: Basal transcription factors are {{c1::proteins eukaryotic RNA polymerase needs to start transcription}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The initiation of transcription by RNA polymerase II requires the assistance of several basal transcription factors."

Parts: basal = at the base, the minimum foundation; every RNA polymerase II promoter needs this set before any regulation is layered on.

Distinguish: enhancers and silencers are DNA sequences (with their own factors) that only tune how efficiently initiation happens; the basal factors are what make initiation possible in the first place.

Formal: "Proteins required for the initiation of transcription in eukaryotes."

Text: Colinear means {{c1::arranged in the same order, unit for unit}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "Most of the well-characterized genes of prokaryotes consist of continuous sequences of nucleotide pairs, which specify colinear sequences of amino acids in the polypeptide gene products."

Parts: co- (together) + linear (in a line): two chains whose units line up in matching order.

Distinguish: a eukaryotic gene split by introns is not colinear with its polypeptide; the DNA carries stretches that never appear in the protein.

Formal: "A relationship in which the units in one molecule occur in the same sequence as the units in another molecule which they specify; for example, the nucleotides in a gene are colinear with the amino acids in the polypeptide encoded by that gene."
verified_against: glossary p610: 'Colinearity (adj., colinear): A relationship in which the units in one molecule occur in the same sequence as the units in another molecule which they specify; for example, the nucleotides in a gene are colinear with the amino acids in the polypeptide encoded by that gene.' | Ex p291: 'Most of the well-characterized genes of prokaryotes consist of continuous sequences of nucleotide pairs, which specify colinear sequences of amino acids in the polypeptide gene products.' | Distinguish p291: 'Most eukaryotic genes contain noncoding sequences called introns that interrupt the coding sequences, or exons.'
